messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amara is a 20-year-old Ethiopian-American woman who works as a pharmacist at a busy urban pharmacy. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 69, reflecting severe and pervasive post-traumatic stress symptoms following an episode of torture she endured approximately fourteen months ago while visiting extended family in her country of origin. She is currently in a relationship and has been living with her partner since returning to the United States, though the relationship has grown strained in ways she finds difficult to articulate.

The events that brought Amara to treatment occurred during a period of civil unrest. She and several relatives were detained by a paramilitary group and held for what she estimates was several days, though her sense of time during that period remains fragmented. During her captivity, Amara was restrained with her arms forced behind her body and submerged repeatedly in a large barrel of water as a method of coercion — her captors demanding information she did not have. She was not alone; others were subjected to the same treatment in her presence. Some of those people did not survive. Amara was eventually released, the precise circumstances of which she cannot fully recall.

She returned to the United States and resumed her pharmacy training within weeks, believing that returning to routine was the correct thing to do. For a time, she managed. But the symptoms that had been present from the beginning — the fragmented sleep, the hypervigilance — did not recede. Instead, they deepened and ramified into her daily life in ways that now feel inescapable.

Water has become one of the most reliably distressing features of Amara's environment. She lives in a city with a river running through it, and her commute to the pharmacy takes her across a bridge each morning. She has not been able to explain to her partner why she began taking a longer route to work months ago. At the pharmacy itself, the sound of the sink running in the back dispensary — a mundane, constant presence in her workday — can stop her mid-task. In those moments, she feels her arms draw back involuntarily, her shoulders pulling inward and behind her as though her body is returning somewhere her mind cannot fully name. The memory, when it surfaces, does not come as a coherent story she can tell herself. It comes as posture, as pressure, as sensation without language. She has tried to describe it to her partner once and found that no words arrived. She has not tried again.

Arguments of any kind — between colleagues at the pharmacy, between customers at the counter — produce an immediate and overwhelming need to locate the nearest exit. Before she enters any room, she has already noted where the doors are. She does this at work, at her partner's family gatherings, in restaurants. She does it without deciding to. At night, she avoids falling asleep for as long as possible, remaining alert in the dark in a way that exhausts her and that she understands, on some level, cannot be sustained. She has begun avoiding the late-afternoon hours that seem most reliably to precede the worst nights.

She no longer attends the Ethiopian Orthodox church her family has worshipped at for decades, because she recognized the face of a man there — someone who had been present during her detention — or believed she did. She cannot be certain. The uncertainty does not make it easier to go back.

What is perhaps most corrosive is what Amara believes about herself in relation to what happened. She is certain that she must remain on guard at all times, and equally certain that she cannot afford to examine the event too directly — that doing so would undo her in some irreversible way. She carries, beneath both of these convictions, a guilt she has not named to anyone: that she survived and others did not, and that this fact implicates her in something she deserves to carry. She tells herself, in quiet moments, that suffering is appropriate. That it is owed.

What finally brought her to seek help was a dispensing error at work — the first of her career — which she attributes to her inability to concentrate. She is afraid, above all, that she is becoming unreliable. What she hopes for, though she offers it tentatively, is simply to feel less like the danger has followed her home.
